title: Six-stitch cable scarf
subtitle: A wide six-stitch rope cable flanked by deep rib panels.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat with a central six-stitch rope cable flanked by 2x2 rib panels on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 22 cm wide by 180 cm long. The cable cross happens every eight rows, giving a slower, more dramatic rope than a four-row repeat, and the flanking ribs keep the sides from spreading.
sourceNotes: Wide rope cable with flanking rib appears in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive, as a standard cabled comforter scarf. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) documents the six-stitch cable construction, citations only.

glossaryTerms.definition: Slip 3 stitches to a cable needle and hold at the front of the work. Knit the next 3 stitches from the left needle. Knit the 3 stitches from the cable needle. The cable crosses to the left.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.
Holding a steam iron above the finished piece to allow steam to open the fabric without pressing down. Preferred for cables to preserve their relief.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat with a centred
C6F

rope cable flanked by 2x2 rib panels on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 22 cm wide and 180 cm long. The cable cross happens on row 1 of an eight-row repeat, giving a slower progression than a four-row cable and a visibly larger arch between each twist. The 2x2 rib at each side keeps the scarf from spreading and adds elasticity to the long edges.

Flat construction was chosen because a cabled and ribbed scarf worked flat needs no seam and lies neatly when cast off and blocked. The finished scarf needs about 400 m (approximately 230 g) of aran-weight yarn. The cable and rib together pull the width in from the raw cast-on, so the 42-stitch cast-on produces a 22 cm wide fabric rather than the 23 cm a plain stocking-stitch swatch would give.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Wool gives crisp cable definition. Any aran-weight yarn works.

items.name: 5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 6 / US 8)

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. In the cable-and-rib fabric the gauge pulls in to approximately 16 sts per 10 cm. Swatch the full arrangement (rib + cable + rib) unstretched, measure dry. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by about 1.4 cm. Row gauge drift across the full 396 rows changes the finished length by up to 15 cm.
Stitches used
K (knit), P (purl), C6F: slip 3 stitches to cable needle held at front, K3 from left needle, K3 from cable needle. 2x2 rib: [K2, P2] repeated across rib panels.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 42 stitches on the needle. Stitch layout: [K2, P2] x 4 (16 sts rib), P2 (purl column), K6 (cable), P2 (purl column), [K2, P2] x 4 (16 sts rib) = 16 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 16 = 42 sts. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 42 stitches: (15.7 x 42) / 10 + 15 = 65.9 + 15 = about 81 cm. Leave a tail of at least 81 cm.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 42 stitches on the needle.
Body
Row 1 (RS, cable row): [K2, P2] 4 times, P2, C6F, P2, [K2, P2] 4 times. (42 sts)
Row 2 (WS): [P2, K2] 4 times, K2, P6, K2, [P2, K2] 4 times. (42 sts)
Rows 3-8 (RS plain and WS): Repeat row 1 without the C6F (knit the cable stitches plain on RS rows) and row 2 pattern on WS rows.
Repeat the 8-row cable repeat until the scarf measures 180 cm. At the halfway mark (approximately row 198, around 90 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 198 you should have 42 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a stretchy bind-off in pattern on a right-side row. The stretchy bind-off preserves the rib elasticity at the bound-off edge and keeps it from flaring narrower than the cast-on edge.
Common faults

Rib alignment shifting after several repeats. If a right-side row is begun on a wrong-side orientation, the rib columns shift by one stitch. Mark the RS with a removable stitch marker before row 1 and always check which side is facing before starting a new row.
Cable cross missing on an eighth row. With an 8-row repeat, keeping track is important. Use a row counter or mark every cross row as you complete it.

Purl columns beside the cable pulling tighter than the rib. The two purl stitches separating the cable from the rib can tighten if worked at the same tension as the purl stitches inside the rib. Consciously work those four stitches (P2 + P2) at a slightly looser tension on right-side rows.
Finishing
Weave in both tails along the back of the rib panel and trim close.
Steam blocking
lifts the cable and opens the rib. Hold the iron above the surface without touching the cable panel. Steam the rib panels more firmly to open them to their full width.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry. Do not tumble dry or stretch the scarf lengthwise while damp.
What to try next

The cable-and-rib scarf combines a different cable arrangement with a more complex rib structure. For a purely cabled surface with no rib, the simple cable scarf removes the flanking rib panels and uses the full width for a reverse stocking stitch ground.
